title: Research Data and Repositories
answer: FAIR data, metadata and ontologies, federated sharing, institutional knowledge graphs and long-term preservation.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: FAIR Data
children.blurb: FAIR data refers to research data and digital objects that are Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable by both people and machines.

children.name: Metadata and Ontologies
children.blurb: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories cover the structured descriptions that make datasets, papers, models and tools findable, comparable and reusable.

children.name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
children.blurb: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers methods for research institutions to jointly analyze or train models on restricted datasets without moving raw records to a central repository.

children.name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
children.blurb: Institutional knowledge graphs are structured representations of an organization's entities, documents, people, projects, datasets, and their relationships, maintained by a university, library, or research institute.

children.name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
children.blurb: Long-term digital preservation is the set of policies, technologies and practices that keep research data and repository objects readable, usable and authentic for decades or longer.

sections.body: Artificial intelligence in research data and repositories is mostly doing practical, unglamorous work. It reads large collections of papers and datasets to suggest keywords, extract structured claims, and link authors to institutions. It aligns metadata fields across different databases so a search in one system can find records stored in another. It builds ontologies by clustering terms that appear together in the literature and flagging synonyms. It also helps with de-identification of sensitive records before they are shared, and it checks file formats for signs of decay in long-term archives. None of this is autonomous; a person still reviews and corrects the output.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Automated metadata extraction is reliable for clean, well-formatted documents like journal articles, but it struggles with scanned pages, handwritten notes, and domain-specific shorthand. Ontology alignment has improved for large, established fields, yet small or fast-moving research areas still require manual curation. Federated sharing of sensitive data has working technical protocols, but legal and institutional trust remain the real bottlenecks. Long-term preservation tools can detect bit rot and format obsolescence, but they cannot guarantee that future software will understand today's data. The site's own library of 135 research papers and 11,222 extracted claims is a small example of what is possible, and it still needs human checking.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with FAIR Data, which sets out the basic requirements for findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable records. Metadata and Ontologies then explains the controlled vocabularies and schemas that make those requirements concrete. Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data addresses the special case where records cannot simply be copied into one place, covering privacy-preserving queries and access controls. Institutional Knowledge Graphs shows how an organisation can connect its people, projects, publications, and datasets into a single queryable structure. Long-Term Digital Preservation closes the loop by asking what happens to all of this in ten, twenty, or fifty years, when formats and institutions change.
